title: Africa’s green industrial future: processing is not enough
body:
To truly gain from green industrialization, green mineral–endowed African countries must think beyond extraction—and beyond processing.

Too often, African countries are offered a narrow role in the green transition: extract here, process a little, export the rest.

That path creates activity—but not industrial power.

Real industrial power lies in building end-to-end value chains. We have seen this clearly with China: the strategic focus was not just on moving up the mineral value chain, but on building capabilities in the technologies that depend on those minerals as critical inputs.

End-to-end value chains entails functional upgrading along the mineral value chain and mastering production, manufacturing, servicing, and eventually innovation in downstream technologies.

Beyond building industrial power, this is also how countries future-proof themselves.

Technology substitution is real.

Resources are not fixed—they become.

This means the window of opportunity offered by today’s green minerals is not infinite. Countries that remain stuck at extraction or basic processing risk being left behind as technologies evolve.

End-to-end value chains place countries on a steep learning curve because firms, workers, and institutions are continuously exposed to production challenges across extraction, processing, manufacturing, deployment, and maintenance, forcing rapid skill accumulation, technological adaptation, and productivity gains that cannot emerge from isolated activities.

Way Forward

- End-to-end value chains require demand at scale, something that no single African country can generate alone.
- This is why regional demand under the AfCFTA is decisive. It allows firms to invest across the full value chain.

Green industrialization will not be won at the mine or the processing plant alone.

- It will be won where markets, skills, and production connect across the entire value chain.

The real question for Africa’s green industrial future is not: “Can Africa process more?”

- The real question is: “Can Africa build and sustain complete green value chains at scale?”
- This is how Africa moves from participation to value capture in the green economy.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D. Godsway K Tetteh, Ph.D
